passage_changes.passage: The anti-defection framework exists to discourage legislators from switching sides. The rules sit in a schedule of the Constitution and cover members of both Parliament and State legislatures. Their aim is to keep governments stable and to make legislators accountable for their conduct. Not every departure is treated the same way, however. The law treats independent members and nominated members differently, depending on when they choose to join a party. Political parties enforce discipline through whips, which direct members how to vote, and the law links defiance of those whips to possible loss of membership. The framework also allows whole groups of members to combine with another party under certain conditions, a feature critics say can encourage large-scale movement between parties. Decisions on these cases are taken by the presiding officer of each house, and courts review those decisions in limited ways. Judges have stressed that such decisions should not be delayed indefinitely, while commentators continue to question whether presiding officers can act impartially when they belong to the ruling party. The debate reflects a wider tension between stable government and the independence that individual legislators may want to exercise.

Reporters Without Borders (RSF) has released the World Press Freedom Index 2026, the 24th edition of its annual report. The Index measures the level of freedom available to journalists in each country and region, and this year it covers 180 countries. Rankings are shaped by legal protections, the diversity of media outlets and the extent of political interference. Each country receives a score on a fixed scale, and the results show sharp contrasts. Some states remain at the top of the table, while others sit at the bottom with severe restrictions on reporters. Between these extremes, many countries have moved up or down because of changes in government or pressure on news organisations. Regions also differ greatly, and journalists in some parts of the world face far greater danger than others. The national questionnaire behind the Index asks experts about the political, legal, economic, social and security environment in each country. Its findings suggest that a free press is closely linked to informed public debate in any society.

National Technology Day is observed every year on 11 May. The day commemorates technological achievements reached on 11 May 1998, when several milestones were reached. One of these was a series of nuclear tests conducted at the Pokhran Test Range in Rajasthan. India had earlier carried out a nuclear test at the same range, and the 1998 tests marked a major step in the country's scientific history. Students preparing for current affairs should be clear about the sequence of these events, the people who led them, and the names given to the operations. The 1998 tests were not the only technological milestones of that day. Another was the first successful test flight of the Hansa-3 aircraft, which marked progress in indigenous aviation. The Defence Research and Development Organisation also carried out a test of the Trishul missile, a short-range surface-to-air weapon. Together these events show why the day is linked with self-reliance in technology. The day has been observed every year since the government began marking it in 1999. Preparation tip: when reading about nuclear and technology milestones, note the day, the number of tests in each series, and the codename used for each operation. Such details are easy to confuse, and they are often asked directly. Keeping a short table of dates and events makes revision faster.

Labour welfare in India is shaped by two sources of authority: the Constitution and a body of ordinary statutes. The Constitution does not only grant rights to individuals; it also sets out aims that the State is expected to pursue. Some provisions protect workers from being made to work against their will, while others shield young people from early employment. Other provisions describe the kind of economic life the State should aim for, including a means of livelihood, employment within economic capacity, fair pay and a voice for workers in the industries where they work. Statutes have translated many of these aims into laws covering factories, wages, provident funds, compensation and disputes between employers and employees. Several of these statutes have since been grouped into a smaller number of broad codes. The codes group rules on wages, industrial relations, social security and occupational safety and health. Each statute addresses a specific aspect of work, such as the payment of wages, the settlement of disputes or compensation to workers. Labour matters also have an international dimension, since a United Nations agency works to improve labour conditions and living standards across the world. Together, these provisions and laws show that labour protection in India has both a constitutional foundation and a statutory one.

Southeast Asia is home to a regional grouping that has become central to how countries in the region manage their relations with one another and with major outside powers. Its members have long preferred a cautious style of diplomacy, in which governments avoid commenting on or interfering in each other's domestic affairs. Leaders and ministers meet through a network of regional forums that cover trade, politics and security, and several of these meetings now include partners from outside the region. The group has also tried to deepen economic ties, aiming to make trade, investment and the movement of people easier across national borders. Its record is not without difficulty. A dispute over a busy sea route has remained unresolved for years, and the group has been criticised for its limited response to a political crisis inside one of its member states. For India, the region has a special importance. New Delhi has built deep political, economic and security ties with the grouping over many years, and its own regional outreach policy places the grouping at the heart of its approach to the wider Indo-Pacific. The group's ability to act together will shape how much influence it can exercise in the years ahead.

Governance in India is judged at several levels, and each level has tools to measure performance. At the village level, a national framework assesses how well local bodies deliver rural services. Rather than offering a simple ranking, it places each body into a category based on a composite score, so officials can see where improvement is needed. The framework is also linked to global development goals, which connects local priorities to wider targets for sustainable growth. Accurate measurement depends on good data. Government statistics agencies run regular surveys of economic activity, including enterprises that are not registered as companies. Such data is useful for planning because it captures sectors that formal records often miss. Finally, oversight of public money rests with Parliament. A committee drawn from both Houses examines how the government spends money and studies reports prepared by the country's audit institution. Its members are chosen in a way that reflects the balance of political parties, which gives the committee its credibility. This oversight protects financial discipline in public spending. Together, these mechanisms show how measurement, statistics and legislative scrutiny support accountability in public administration.

India's external engagement now reaches small businesses abroad, labour rights at home and the working of central banks. Subrahmanyam Jaishankar inaugurated India-supported projects in Trinidad and Tobago under an initiative that supplies equipment to small and medium enterprises in countries of the Global South. The programme is an Indian developmental cooperation initiative, so its benefits flow to partner countries.

Labour standards also came into focus when tea plantation workers in West Bengal raised allegations of violations in tea estates. The allegations concern conditions inside the tea estates themselves. Their complaint was taken to an international body that holds member countries accountable for implementing ratified conventions. Tea itself is governed by a national board that regulates cultivation, production, sale and export.

On the financial side, the Reserve Bank of India and the European Central Bank have revised a memorandum of understanding, which means an earlier arrangement between them has now been updated. The aim is to enhance cooperation in banking supervision and financial regulation. The euro area is a group of European Union countries that use the euro as their official currency, and its central bank sits at the centre of this cooperation. Over the years, the euro area has expanded as more countries adopted the currency, and additions have come in different years.

The Places of Worship Act, 1991 was passed by a Congress government to protect the religious identity of places of worship. Its central aim is to keep the religious character of each place as it stood on Independence Day. The Act prohibits converting a place of worship from one religious denomination to another, whether between or within denominations. It terminates pending legal proceedings about religious character conversions that took place before the cut-off, while allowing new cases about changes made after it. Violating the Act attracts imprisonment and fines. The Act exempts ancient monuments protected under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, and it does not cover the Ayodhya dispute and related legal proceedings. Critics argue that the Act limits judicial review, weakening constitutional checks and balances. Others say that it violates the right to freedom of religion and treats communities differently, undermining equality. Critics also argue that the Independence Day cut-off ignores historical injustices and earlier encroachments. The Supreme Court, in its verdict on the Ayodhya dispute, said that the Act upholds secular values and prohibits retrogression. Its supporters say the Act ensures the preservation of religious sites and their character, instilling confidence in all communities. Together, these points explain why the Act remains a contested law.

Judges of the Supreme Court are appointed by the President, and the Constitution lays down the qualifications a person must have before appointment. A candidate must be a citizen of India and must meet one of several experience-based or distinguished-jurist criteria. Once in office, a judge does not serve a fixed term. Instead, the judge continues until reaching a set retirement age, and may also choose to leave earlier by writing to the President. The Constitution provides a formal route for removal, which is demanding. Removal is permitted only on the grounds of proven misbehaviour or incapacity. A special law governs the procedure, and the same process applies to judges of the Supreme Court and of the High Courts. Several judges have faced removal motions in Parliament, and in some cases the motion failed or the judge resigned before the process was complete. The question of who should decide appointments has been debated for decades, and Court rulings have repeatedly reshaped the process. Consultation between the Chief Justice and other senior judges sits at the heart of that debate. These disputes show how closely appointments and removals are linked to judicial independence.

Some international bodies are created to set common standards rather than to govern countries directly. The body discussed here is one of them, and its concern is the working life of people across the world. It was set up under the Treaty of Versailles and was later linked with the United Nations. Its central aim is to improve labour conditions and living standards throughout the world. Its structure gives an equal voice to three groups: governments, employers and workers. The organisation has four stated objectives. It seeks to promote fundamental labour rights, create greater opportunities for women and men, enhance social protection and strengthen social dialogue. Its legal instruments take two forms. Conventions and Protocols are legally binding treaties, while Recommendations are non-binding guidelines. Some of its standards form part of the wider United Nations human rights framework. The organisation also publishes reports on employment, wages, social protection and youth. Its Director General leads the organisation's work. The work covers workers in many countries, including India, which is one of its founding members. Taken together, these standards and reports show how an international body can influence labour conditions.

Human-elephant conflict is a serious concern for communities living near elephant habitats, and it affects both people and the animals. Retaliatory violence is one of its most harmful forms, and the response combines several measures that work on the ground and in research. The central government runs a national programme that protects elephants, conserves their habitats and maintains the corridors they use to move. A state has now decided to create a dedicated research centre on this conflict.

Other measures focus on people and their livelihoods. Public awareness drives, community sensitisation and conservation education are meant to reduce retaliatory violence. One method uses bees to reduce elephant-human attacks, and it is run by a national body that supports village industries. A separate public campaign encourages coexistence between humans and elephants.

Weather and air also need careful observation in cities. Under Mission Mausam, an urban testbed and aerosol observatory has been inaugurated in a city. Its work is linked with a Chennai-based research institute. The facility observes urban weather in real time, tracks air quality and aerosols, and supports climate-related research. The facility works in an urban setting, where weather and air observation are tracked in one system.
